title: Ἀχιλλῆος τεύχεα
about: Menelaus gives ground before Hector’s Trojans, like a lion driven from the farmyard, and finds Ajax on the left of the battle, where Apollo has cast flight among the Achaeans. He calls him to help save the body of Patroclus, and Ajax stands over it like a lion over his cubs, with Menelaus on the other side. Hector has stripped Patroclus’ armour and means to cut off the head and give the body to the dogs; when Ajax comes up he withdraws, sending the armour toward Troy. Glaucus, the Lycian leader, rebukes him for fleeing from Ajax and for leaving Sarpedon to the dogs; Hector answers that Zeus decides who wins, and bids Glaucus watch. He rallies his men, runs after the armour-bearers, and puts on the divine armour of Achilles, which the gods gave to Peleus and Peleus to his son.

sentences.t:
εἷος ὁ ταῦθ’ ὅρμαινε κατὰ φρένα καὶ κατὰ θυμὸν
τόφρα δ’ ἐπὶ Τρώων στίχες ἤλυθον·
sentences.l:
While he these things was pondering in mind and in heart,
meanwhile came on the ranks of the Trojans;
sentences.i: While he was turning these things over in his mind and heart, the ranks of the Trojans came on;
sentences.n: εἷος ὁ ταῦθ’ ὅρμαινε takes up Menelaus’ debate with himself (17.91–105): εἷος is the epic form of ἕως ‘while’, answered by τόφρα ‘meanwhile’; ὁ is the pronoun ‘he’, ταῦθ’ is ταῦτα elided, and ὅρμαινε is an unaugmented imperfect of ὁρμαίνω ‘turn over in the mind’. κατὰ φρένα καὶ κατὰ θυμόν ‘in mind and in heart’ is a stock phrase for thinking something through. ἐπὶ … ἤλυθον is tmesis, the preverb standing apart from the aorist (Attic ἐπῆλθον), ‘came on’; Τρώων στίχες ‘the ranks of the Trojans’ is the subject.

sentences.t: ἦρχε δ’ ἄρ’ Ἕκτωρ.
sentences.l: and led them, then, Hector.
sentences.i: and Hector led them.
sentences.n: ἦρχε is the imperfect of ἄρχω ‘lead’. ἄρ’ (= ἄρα) is the connecting particle ‘then’: the Trojan ranks come on behind Hector, and his leading is what drives Menelaus back in the next lines.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὅ γ’ ἐξοπίσω ἀνεχάζετο, λεῖπε δὲ νεκρὸν
ἐντροπαλιζόμενος ὥς τε λὶς ἠϋγένειος,
ὅν ῥα κύνες τε καὶ ἄνδρες ἀπὸ σταθμοῖο δίωνται
ἔγχεσι καὶ φωνῇ·
sentences.l:
But he to the rear was drawing back, and was leaving the corpse,
turning back again and again, like a fine-bearded lion,
whom dogs and men from the steading chase off
with spears and with a shout;
sentences.i: But he kept drawing back toward the rear, leaving the corpse, turning to look back again and again, like a fine-bearded lion that dogs and men chase off from the steading with spears and shouting;
sentences.n: The subject is Menelaus, giving up the body to the Trojans, and the sentence turns into a simile at ὥς τε ‘just as’. ἀνεχάζετο ‘was drawing back’ and ἐξοπίσω ‘to the rear’ come together; λεῖπε is an unaugmented imperfect, ‘was leaving’. ἐντροπαλιζόμενος ‘turning back again and again’ is a frequentative built on τρέπω: he keeps looking behind him as he goes. λίς is a poetic word for ‘lion’, and ἠϋγένειος ‘fine-bearded’ is made of ἠΰς ‘fine’ and γένειον ‘beard’ (the diaeresis is as printed). δίωνται is a subjunctive meaning ‘chase off’ (from δίεμαι), with no κε because the simile states what happens whenever it happens. ὅν ῥα: ῥα is a particle that adds liveliness and is not translated. σταθμός is the steading where the herds are kept.

sentences.t:
τοῦ δ’ ἐν φρεσὶν ἄλκιμον ἦτορ
παχνοῦται, ἀέκων δέ τ’ ἔβη ἀπὸ μεσσαύλοιο·
sentences.l:
and of him in his wits the valiant heart
is chilled, and unwilling he went from the farmyard;
sentences.i: and the valiant heart within him is chilled, and unwilling he goes off from the farmyard;
sentences.n: The simile goes on with the lion, and τοῦ is ‘his’. ἄλκιμον ἦτορ ‘valiant heart’ is the heart that makes it bold. παχνοῦται (from πάχνη ‘hoarfrost’) is ‘is chilled, is stiffened’; the picture is of courage going cold in the animal at the dogs and the spears. ἀέκων ‘unwilling’ is the lion’s reluctance. δέ τ’ (epic τε) marks what is always so, and ἔβη, an aorist, is gnomic: in English a present, ‘goes’. μεσσαύλοιο ‘farmyard’ is the yard in the middle of a farmstead.

sentences.t: ὣς ἀπὸ Πατρόκλοιο κίε ξανθὸς Μενέλαος.
sentences.l: So from Patroclus went fair-haired Menelaus.
sentences.i: So fair-haired Menelaus went away from Patroclus.
sentences.n: ὣς ‘so’ closes the simile and points back to the lion: Menelaus goes as unwillingly as the beast. κίε is an unaugmented imperfect of κίω ‘go’. ξανθός ‘fair-haired’ is Menelaus’ stock epithet and is translated every time.

sentences.t:
στῆ δὲ μεταστρεφθεὶς ἐπεὶ ἵκετο ἔθνος ἑταίρων
παπταίνων Αἴαντα μέγαν Τελαμώνιον υἱόν.
sentences.l:
and he stood, having turned about, when he came to the company of his companions,
glancing about for Ajax, great Telamonian son.
sentences.i: He turned and halted when he reached the company of his companions, glancing about for Ajax, Telamon’s great son.
sentences.n: στῆ is an unaugmented aorist, ‘stood, halted’, and μεταστρεφθείς, the aorist passive participle of μεταστρέφω, ‘having turned round’. ἔθνος ἑταίρων is ‘the company of his companions’: ἔθνος here is a body of people, not a ‘nation’. παπταίνων ‘glancing about’ takes Αἴαντα as its object, ‘looking about for’. μέγαν Τελαμώνιον υἱόν ‘great Telamonian son’ picks out which Ajax is meant, the son of Telamon.

sentences.t:
τὸν δὲ μάλ’ αἶψ’ ἐνόησε μάχης ἐπ’ ἀριστερὰ πάσης
θαρσύνονθ’ ἑτάρους καὶ ἐποτρύνοντα μάχεσθαι·
sentences.l:
And him very quickly he noticed, on the left of all the battle,
cheering his companions and urging them on to fight;
sentences.i: And he very soon noticed him on the left of the whole battle, cheering his companions and urging them on to fight;
sentences.n: τὸν δέ ‘and him’ is Ajax, the object of ἐνόησε ‘noticed’ (unaugmented aorist). μάχης ἐπ’ ἀριστερὰ πάσης ‘on the left of all the battle’ gives his place on the field. θαρσύνονθ’ is θαρσύνοντα elided, ‘cheering’; ἑτάρους is the shortened form of ἑταίρους ‘companions’; ἐποτρύνοντα μάχεσθαι ‘urging on to fight’. Line 117 is word for word the line used of Alexander at 13.767.

sentences.t: θεσπέσιον γάρ σφιν φόβον ἔμβαλε Φοῖβος Ἀπόλλων·
sentences.l: for wondrous flight on them cast Phoebus Apollo;
sentences.i: for Phoebus Apollo had cast wondrous flight among them;
sentences.n: γάρ explains why Ajax is having to cheer his men on: ἔμβαλε (unaugmented aorist of ἐμβάλλω ‘throw in’) says that Apollo had thrown φόβον, ‘flight’, among them, and σφιν is the dative plural ‘them’, the men Ajax is cheering. φόβος in battle is flight, the running that fear drives, so the god has put flight into the men. θεσπέσιον ‘wondrous’ is the stock adjective for what exceeds ordinary measure. Φοῖβος Ἀπόλλων ‘Phoebus Apollo’ is a standing name for the god.

sentences.t: βῆ δὲ θέειν, εἶθαρ δὲ παριστάμενος ἔπος ηὔδα.
sentences.l: and he went to run, and at once, standing beside him, spoke a word:
sentences.i: He set off running, and at once, standing beside Ajax, said:
sentences.n: βῆ is an unaugmented aorist, and βῆ δὲ θέειν ‘he went to run’ is an idiom for ‘set off running’; θέειν is the uncontracted infinitive of θέω ‘run’ (Attic θεῖν). εἶθαρ ‘at once’; παριστάμενος ‘standing beside’. ἔπος ηὔδα ‘spoke a word’ is the formula that introduces a speech, and the speaker is Menelaus.

sentences.t:
Αἶαν δεῦρο πέπον, περὶ Πατρόκλοιο θανόντος
σπεύσομεν, αἴ κε νέκυν περ Ἀχιλλῆϊ προφέρωμεν
γυμνόν·
sentences.i: “Ajax, come here, my good fellow, and let us hasten for the sake of dead Patroclus, in case we may carry his body at least to Achilles, stripped;
sentences.n: Αἶαν is the vocative of Αἴας, and δεῦρο ‘here’ is a summons. πέπον ‘good one’ is a form of address whose meaning is not known; it reads as friendly and urgent. περὶ Πατρόκλοιο θανόντος ‘about dead Patroclus’: περί with the genitive means ‘for the sake of’, and θανόντος is the aorist participle ‘who has died’. σπεύσομεν looks like a future but is probably a short-vowel subjunctive, ‘let us hasten’. αἴ κε (= εἰ with κε) with the subjunctive προφέρωμεν ‘we may carry forward’ is ‘in case we can carry’; νέκυν περ ‘the corpse at least’, and γυμνόν ‘naked’ is said of the body: the armour is gone.

sentences.t: ἀτὰρ τά γε τεύχε’ ἔχει κορυθαίολος Ἕκτωρ.
sentences.l: but the armour, that, has Hector of the glancing helmet.”
sentences.i: but Hector of the glancing helmet has the armour.”
sentences.n: ἀτάρ ‘but’ turns from the naked body to the armour: ἀτὰρ τά γε τεύχε’ ἔχει ‘but those pieces of armour Hector has’, with γε pointing at τά ‘those’ and τεύχε’ for τεύχεα. κορυθαίολος ‘of the glancing helmet’ is Hector’s stock epithet, from κόρυς ‘helmet’ and αἰόλος ‘quick-moving, glancing’. The speech ends here, at the edition’s full stop.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφατ’, Αἴαντι δὲ δαΐφρονι θυμὸν ὄρινε·
sentences.l: So he spoke, and in Ajax, wise-minded, the spirit he stirred;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and he stirred the spirit of wise-hearted Ajax;
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφατ’ ‘so he spoke’ (ἔφατ’ for ἔφατο) closes the speech. The dative Αἴαντι … δαΐφρονι is a dative of the person affected, ‘in wise-minded Ajax’, with θυμόν the part stirred, and ὄρινε is the aorist of ὀρίνω ‘stir up, rouse’, here without augment. δαΐφρων is rendered ‘wise-minded’ in the first layer and ‘wise-hearted’ in the second everywhere, though whether it means ‘wise’ or ‘fierce’ is disputed.

sentences.t: βῆ δὲ διὰ προμάχων, ἅμα δὲ ξανθὸς Μενέλαος.
sentences.l: and he went through the front-fighters, and along with him fair-haired Menelaus.
sentences.i: He went through the foremost fighters, and fair-haired Menelaus went with him.
sentences.n: βῆ is an unaugmented aorist. Its subject, Ajax, is not named again, but the dative Αἴαντι in the line before makes him the one who goes. διὰ προμάχων ‘through the front-fighters’ are the champions who fight ahead of the main body. ἅμα here is an adverb, ‘at the same time, together’, and puts Menelaus at Ajax’s side.

sentences.t:
Ἕκτωρ μὲν Πάτροκλον ἐπεὶ κλυτὰ τεύχε’ ἀπηύρα,
ἕλχ’ ἵν’ ἀπ’ ὤμοιιν κεφαλὴν τάμοι ὀξέϊ χαλκῷ,
τὸν δὲ νέκυν Τρῳῇσιν ἐρυσσάμενος κυσὶ δοίη.
sentences.l:
Hector, when from Patroclus the famous armour he had taken away,
was dragging him, that from the two shoulders the head he might cut with the sharp bronze,
and the corpse, having dragged it, to the Trojan dogs might give.
sentences.i: Hector, once he had taken the famous armour from Patroclus, was dragging him, to cut the head from his shoulders with the sharp bronze and, having dragged the corpse away, give it to the Trojan dogs.
sentences.n: A narrator’s aside on what Hector has been doing. Ἕκτωρ μέν is answered by Αἴας δ’ in the next line. ἀπαυράω ‘take away’ takes two accusatives, the man and the thing, so ἀπηύρα with Πάτροκλον … τεύχεα is ‘took the armour from Patroclus’. ἕλχ’ is ἕλκε, an unaugmented imperfect ‘was dragging’; the κ becomes χ before the rough breathing of ἵν’. ἵν’ … τάμοι … δοίη are optatives of purpose after a past tense. ὤμοιιν is the dual, ‘the two shoulders’. Τρῳῇσιν is feminine to agree with κυσί, as κύων may be feminine.

sentences.t: Αἴας δ’ ἐγγύθεν ἦλθε φέρων σάκος ἠΰτε πύργον·
sentences.l: And Ajax from close by came, bearing his shield like a tower;
sentences.i: And Ajax came up from close by, carrying a shield like a tower;
sentences.n: The line is the one used at 7.219; there the sentence goes on to describe the shield, here it stops. ἐγγύθεν ‘from close by’; ἠΰτε ‘like’ introduces the comparison, and a shield that is ‘like a tower’ is large enough to stand behind. Αἴας δ’ answers Ἕκτωρ μέν in line 125: Hector draws away while Ajax comes up.

sentences.t:
Ἕκτωρ δ’ ἂψ ἐς ὅμιλον ἰὼν ἀνεχάζεθ’ ἑταίρων,
ἐς δίφρον δ’ ἀνόρουσε·
sentences.l:
and Hector, back into the throng of his companions going, was drawing back,
and into his chariot leapt up;
sentences.i: But Hector, going back into the throng of his companions, drew back, and leapt up into his chariot;
sentences.n: ἂψ ἐς ὅμιλον … ἑταίρων ‘back into the throng of his companions’; ἀνεχάζεθ’ is the imperfect ἀνεχάζετο ‘was drawing back’ (the elided τ is aspirated before the rough breathing of ἑταίρων), the verb Menelaus used of himself at 108. ἀνόρουσε is the aorist of ἀνορούω ‘leap up’, and δίφρον here is the chariot.

sentences.t:
δίδου δ’ ὅ γε τεύχεα καλὰ
Τρωσὶ φέρειν προτὶ ἄστυ, μέγα κλέος ἔμμεναι αὐτῷ.
sentences.l:
and he was giving the fine armour
to the Trojans to carry to the town, to be great glory for himself.
sentences.i: and he handed the fine armour to the Trojans to carry to the town, to be great glory for himself.
sentences.n: δίδου is an unaugmented imperfect of δίδωμι, ‘was giving’. τεύχεα καλά ‘the fine armour’ is what Hector took from Patroclus (line 125), and the Trojans are carrying it at 191. Τρωσὶ φέρειν ‘to the Trojans to carry’ is an infinitive of purpose, and προτὶ is πρός. In μέγα κλέος ἔμμεναι αὐτῷ, ἔμμεναι is εἶναι, ‘to be great glory for him’: the armour carried into the town makes his fame.

sentences.t:
Αἴας δ’ ἀμφὶ Μενοιτιάδῃ σάκος εὐρὺ καλύψας
ἑστήκει ὥς τίς τε λέων περὶ οἷσι τέκεσσιν,
ᾧ ῥά τε νήπι’ ἄγοντι συναντήσωνται ἐν ὕλῃ
ἄνδρες ἐπακτῆρες·
sentences.l:
And Ajax, about Menoetius’-son his wide shield having spread,
was standing like some lion about his own cubs,
to whom, leading his little ones, meet in the wood
men, hunters;
sentences.i: And Ajax stood with his wide shield spread round the son of Menoetius, like a lion about its own cubs, which hunters meet in the wood as it leads its little ones along;
sentences.n: A second simile, for Ajax. ἑστήκει is a pluperfect used for a state, ‘was standing’, and is the main verb: ἀμφὶ Μενοιτιάδῃ σάκος εὐρὺ καλύψας ‘having spread his wide shield about the son of Menoetius’ (Patroclus, by patronymic) says how. Then ὥς τίς τε λέων ‘like some lion’ begins the comparison. οἷσι is the possessive ‘his own’, not a relative, with τέκεσσιν ‘cubs’; ᾧ … ἄγοντι is a dative ‘to whom, as he leads’, and νήπι’ (νήπια) is ‘little ones’, the young, not the ‘foolish’ of νήπιος. συναντήσωνται is a subjunctive, since the simile tells what happens whenever it happens. ἐπακτῆρες ‘hunters’ is from ἐπάγω ‘bring on’.

sentences.t:
ὃ δέ τε σθένεϊ βλεμεαίνει,
πᾶν δέ τ’ ἐπισκύνιον κάτω ἕλκεται ὄσσε καλύπτων·
sentences.l:
and he in his strength exults,
and all the brow downward he draws, his two eyes covering;
sentences.i: and it exults in its strength, and draws its whole brow down, covering its eyes;
sentences.n: The simile continues with the lion as subject: ὃ δέ τε ‘and he’, with the τε of what always happens. σθένεϊ βλεμεαίνει ‘exults in his strength’; the sense of βλεμεαίνω is not certain. ἐπισκύνιον is the skin of the brow, and κάτω ἕλκεται, in the middle voice, is ‘draws down for himself’. ὄσσε is a dual, ‘the two eyes’. The picture is the beast’s scowl, with the brow pulled over the eyes.

sentences.t: ὣς Αἴας περὶ Πατρόκλῳ ἥρωϊ βεβήκει.
sentences.l: So Ajax about Patroclus the hero was standing.
sentences.i: So Ajax stood around the hero Patroclus.
sentences.n: ὣς closes the simile and ties Ajax to the lion. βεβήκει is a pluperfect of βαίνω used for a state, ‘was standing’, and Πατρόκλῳ is the dative with περί, ‘around Patroclus’. ἥρωϊ ‘the hero’ is the title given to the dead man.

sentences.t:
Ἀτρεΐδης δ’ ἑτέρωθεν ἀρηΐφιλος Μενέλαος
ἑστήκει, μέγα πένθος ἐνὶ στήθεσσιν ἀέξων.
sentences.l:
And Atreus’-son, from the other side, Ares-loved Menelaus,
was standing, great grief in his breast increasing.
sentences.i: And on the other side stood the son of Atreus, Menelaus, dear to Ares, letting great grief grow in his breast.
sentences.n: Ἀτρεΐδης here is Menelaus himself, the patronymic standing beside the name, not Agamemnon. ἑτέρωθεν ‘from the other side’ sets him opposite Ajax, and ἑστήκει repeats the verb of line 133 for the second man. ἀρηΐφιλος ‘dear to Ares’ is made of Ἄρης and φίλος. In μέγα πένθος … ἀέξων the participle of ἀέξω ‘make grow’ says he is feeding his grief.

sentences.t:
Γλαῦκος δ’ Ἱππολόχοιο πάϊς Λυκίων ἀγὸς ἀνδρῶν
Ἕκτορ’ ὑπόδρα ἰδὼν χαλεπῷ ἠνίπαπε μύθῳ·
sentences.l:
And Glaucus, Hippolochus’ son, leader of the Lycian men,
at Hector with a scowl looking, with a harsh word rebuked him:
sentences.i: And Glaucus, the son of Hippolochus, leader of the Lycian men, looking at Hector with a scowl, rebuked him with a harsh word:
sentences.n: The new speaker is Glaucus, the Lycian leader, and line 140 is also the line used of him at 7.13. Ἱππολόχοιο πάϊς ‘Hippolochus’ son’ is a patronymic phrase; ἀγὸς ἀνδρῶν ‘leader of men’. Ἕκτορ’ is the object of ἰδών; ὑπόδρα ἰδών ‘looking from under (his brows), with a scowl’ is a formula whose derivation is not certain. ἠνίπαπε is the aorist of ἐνίπτω ‘rebuke’, and χαλεπῷ μύθῳ ‘with a harsh word’ says how.

sentences.t: Ἕκτορ εἶδος ἄριστε μάχης ἄρα πολλὸν ἐδεύεο.
sentences.l: “Hector, in form the best, of battle then much you were lacking.
sentences.i: “Hector, best in form, it seems you were greatly lacking in battle.
sentences.n: Glaucus opens with a taunt. εἶδος ἄριστε ‘best in form’ is a vocative with an accusative of respect, set against μάχης … ἐδεύεο ‘you were lacking in battle’: a man good to look at is not necessarily good at fighting. δεύομαι (= δέομαι) takes the genitive, and ἐδεύεο is the second person imperfect middle with the uncontracted ending -εο (= -ου). ἄρα ‘then, it seems’ marks a discovery, as in line 147. πολλόν is πολύ.

sentences.t: ἦ σ’ αὔτως κλέος ἐσθλὸν ἔχει φύξηλιν ἐόντα.
sentences.l: Truly you just so good glory holds, a runaway being.
sentences.i: Surely it is for nothing that good glory holds you, runaway that you are.
sentences.n: ἦ ‘truly’ opens a sneer, and σ’ is σε. αὔτως ‘just so, for nothing’ says the glory has no ground. ἔχει has κλέος ἐσθλόν ‘good glory’ as its subject and σε as object, ‘holds you’. φύξηλιν ἐόντα ‘being a runaway’ agrees with σ’. φύξηλις is a rare word built on φεύγω ‘flee’ and best taken as ‘one who runs away’; its exact shade is not known.

sentences.t:
φράζεο νῦν ὅππως κε πόλιν καὶ ἄστυ σαώσῃς
οἶος σὺν λαοῖς τοὶ Ἰλίῳ ἐγγεγάασιν·
sentences.l:
Consider now how you may save city and town
alone, with the people who in Ilium have been born;
sentences.i: Think now how you may save city and town, alone, with the people born in Ilium;
sentences.n: φράζεο is the imperative of φράζομαι ‘consider’ with the uncontracted ending -εο (= -ου). ὅππως κε … σαώσῃς ‘how you may save’ is an indirect question with a subjunctive, σαώσῃς from σαόω ‘save’; πόλιν καὶ ἄστυ ‘city and town’ is a pair of near-synonyms. οἶος ‘alone’ agrees with the understood σύ, and τοί is the relative (= οἵ): Hector is to hold Troy with the people born in Ilium only, ἐγγεγάασιν being the perfect ‘have been born in, are native to’, so without the allies, as the next lines say.

sentences.t:
οὐ γάρ τις Λυκίων γε μαχησόμενος Δαναοῖσιν
εἶσι περὶ πτόλιος, ἐπεὶ οὐκ ἄρα τις χάρις ἦεν
μάρνασθαι δηΐοισιν ἐπ’ ἀνδράσι νωλεμὲς αἰεί.
sentences.l:
For no one of the Lycians at least, to fight the Danaans,
will go for the city, since there was, it seems, no gratitude
in fighting against hostile men unceasingly, always.
sentences.i: For no Lycian at least will go to fight the Danaans for the city’s sake, since it seems that there was no gratitude for fighting hostile men without pause, forever.
sentences.n: οὐ γάρ … τις ‘for no one’ gives the reason for the warning. μαχησόμενος is a future participle of purpose, ‘to fight’, with εἶσι (future of εἶμι ‘go’); περὶ πτόλιος ‘for the city’ (πτόλις is the older form of πόλις). ἦεν is ἦν. ἄρα ‘it seems’ marks a conclusion Glaucus has drawn, and χάρις is ‘gratitude’, thanks owed for service. Line 148 repeats the line at 9.317.

sentences.t:
πῶς κε σὺ χείρονα φῶτα σαώσειας μεθ’ ὅμιλον
σχέτλι’, ἐπεὶ Σαρπηδόν’ ἅμα ξεῖνον καὶ ἑταῖρον
κάλλιπες Ἀργείοισιν ἕλωρ καὶ κύρμα γενέσθαι,
sentences.l:
How could you a worse man save in the throng,
cruel one, since Sarpedon, guest-friend and companion alike,
you left behind for the Argives to become prey and spoil,
sentences.i: How could you save a worse man in the throng, cruel one, when you left Sarpedon, both guest-friend and companion, to become prey and spoil for the Argives,
sentences.n: πῶς κε … σαώσειας is a potential optative question, ‘how could you save?’, and χείρονα φῶτα ‘a worse man’ (a man worse than Sarpedon) carries the argument: one who gave up a better man cannot be trusted with a lesser one. σχέτλι’ is the vocative of σχέτλιος ‘cruel one’, an angry address. κάλλιπες is κατέλιπες, the preverb shortened and assimilated. ξεῖνον καὶ ἑταῖρον ‘guest-friend and companion’ are joined by ἅμα ‘at once, alike’. ἕλωρ καὶ κύρμα ‘prey and spoil’ with γενέσθαι ‘to become’ is the pair used at Odyssey 3.271.

sentences.t:
ὅς τοι πόλλ’ ὄφελος γένετο πτόλεΐ τε καὶ αὐτῷ
ζωὸς ἐών· νῦν δ’ οὔ οἱ ἀλαλκέμεναι κύνας ἔτλης.
sentences.l:
who to you much help was, and to the city and to yourself,
being alive; but now not for him to ward off the dogs did you bring yourself.
sentences.i: who was of much use to the city and to you yourself while he lived; but now you did not bring yourself to ward the dogs off him.
sentences.n: ὅς takes up Sarpedon. τοι is the dative ‘to you’ (= σοι), ὄφελος means ‘help, advantage’, and πτόλεΐ τε καὶ αὐτῷ is ‘to the city and to yourself’, αὐτῷ being Hector. ζωὸς ἐών ‘while he was alive’. In νῦν δ’ οὔ οἱ ἀλαλκέμεναι κύνας, οἱ is ‘for him’ and ἀλαλκέμεναι is the infinitive ‘to ward off’ with κύνας ‘the dogs’ as its object. ἔτλης is the aorist of τλάω; with an infinitive it is ‘bring oneself to’.

sentences.t:
τὼ νῦν εἴ τις ἐμοὶ Λυκίων ἐπιπείσεται ἀνδρῶν
οἴκαδ’ ἴμεν, Τροίῃ δὲ πεφήσεται αἰπὺς ὄλεθρος.
sentences.l:
So now, if any of the Lycian men will obey me
to go home, for Troy steep destruction will be shown.
sentences.i: So now, if any of the Lycians will obey me and go home, steep destruction will show itself for Troy.
sentences.n: τὼ is τῷ ‘therefore’. ἐπιπείσεται is the future of ἐπιπείθομαι ‘obey’, with ἐμοί, and ἴμεν is ἰέναι ‘to go’; οἴκαδ’ ‘homeward’. The δέ in Τροίῃ δέ starts the main clause after the ‘if’. πεφήσεται is taken as a reduplicated future passive of φαίνω, ‘will be shown, will appear’; the derivation is not certain, but the sense is not in doubt. αἰπὺς ὄλεθρος ‘steep destruction’ keeps the Greek epithet.

sentences.t:
εἰ γὰρ νῦν Τρώεσσι μένος πολυθαρσὲς ἐνείη
ἄτρομον, οἷόν τ’ ἄνδρας ἐσέρχεται οἳ περὶ πάτρης
ἀνδράσι δυσμενέεσσι πόνον καὶ δῆριν ἔθεντο,
αἶψά κε Πάτροκλον ἐρυσαίμεθα Ἴλιον εἴσω.
sentences.l:
For if now in the Trojans strength much-daring
untrembling were present, such as enters men who for their fatherland
on hostile men toil and contest have set,
quickly Patroclus we might drag into Ilium.
sentences.i: For if the Trojans now had in them a strength of great daring, untrembling, such as enters men who for their fatherland lay toil and contest upon their enemies, we should quickly drag Patroclus into Ilium.
sentences.n: εἰ … ἐνείη (optative of ἔνειμι ‘be in’) gives a condition that is not met, and its main clause is the potential αἶψά κε … ἐρυσαίμεθα ‘we might quickly drag’. μένος πολυθαρσές ‘strength of great daring’ and ἄτρομον ‘untrembling’ describe the strength Glaucus wishes the Trojans had. οἷόν τ’ is οἷον τε ‘such as’, and ἐσέρχεται is a general present ‘enters’. οἳ … ἔθεντο ‘who have set’ is a gnomic aorist, and ἀνδράσι δυσμενέεσσι ‘on hostile men’ is the dative for whom the πόνον καὶ δῆριν ‘toil and contest’ is set; περὶ πάτρης ‘for their fatherland’.

sentences.t:
εἰ δ’ οὗτος προτὶ ἄστυ μέγα Πριάμοιο ἄνακτος
ἔλθοι τεθνηὼς καί μιν ἐρυσαίμεθα χάρμης,
αἶψά κεν Ἀργεῖοι Σαρπηδόνος ἔντεα καλὰ
λύσειαν, καί κ’ αὐτὸν ἀγοίμεθα Ἴλιον εἴσω·
sentences.l:
But if this man to the great town of Priam, the lord,
were to come, dead, and we were to drag him out of the joy of battle,
quickly the Argives Sarpedon’s fine gear
would release, and himself we might lead into Ilium;
sentences.i: But if this man were to come, dead, to the great town of lord Priam, and we were to drag him out of the joy of battle, the Argives would quickly give up Sarpedon’s fine gear, and we might lead the man himself into Ilium;
sentences.n: οὗτος ‘this man’ is Patroclus, and the optatives ἔλθοι ‘were to come’ and ἐρυσαίμεθα ‘we were to drag’ continue the unfulfilled condition. τεθνηώς is the perfect participle ‘dead’. προτὶ ἄστυ μέγα Πριάμοιο ἄνακτος ‘to the great town of lord Priam’. μιν ἐρυσαίμεθα χάρμης takes the genitive of the place dragged from, ‘out of the joy of battle’. The main clause is αἶψά κεν … λύσειαν ‘the Argives would quickly release’, λύω being ‘loose, release’ as one releases something in a ransom, with Σαρπηδόνος ἔντεα καλά ‘Sarpedon’s fine gear’, and καί κ’ αὐτὸν ἀγοίμεθα ‘and we might lead off Sarpedon himself’. The picture is an exchange of the bodies, with the armour.

sentences.t:
τοίου γὰρ θεράπων πέφατ’ ἀνέρος, ὃς μέγ’ ἄριστος
Ἀργείων παρὰ νηυσὶ καὶ ἀγχέμαχοι θεράποντες.
sentences.l:
for of such a man an attendant has been slain, who is by far the best
of the Argives at the ships, and close-fighting attendants.
sentences.i: for the attendant of such a man has been slain, a man who is by far the best of the Argives at the ships, and who has close-fighting attendants.
sentences.n: τοίου γάρ gives the reason the Argives would pay: ‘for the attendant of such a man’. πέφατ’ is πέφαται, the perfect passive of φένω ‘kill’, ‘has been slain’, and θεράπων is the ‘attendant’ Patroclus; ‘such a man’ is Achilles, though the Greek does not name him. ὃς μέγ’ ἄριστος Ἀργείων παρὰ νηυσί ‘who is by far the best of the Argives at the ships’. In καὶ ἀγχέμαχοι θεράποντες the verb is left out, ‘and (he has) close-fighting attendants’. Line 165 is the line at 16.272.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ σύ γ’ Αἴαντος μεγαλήτορος οὐκ ἐτάλασσας
στήμεναι ἄντα κατ’ ὄσσε ἰδὼν δηΐων ἐν ἀϋτῇ,
οὐδ’ ἰθὺς μαχέσασθαι, ἐπεὶ σέο φέρτερός ἐστι.
sentences.l:
But you, of Ajax, great-spirited, did not dare
to stand against him, looking him in the eyes, in the battle-cry of enemies,
nor to fight him straight on, since than you stronger he is.”
sentences.i: But you did not dare to stand against great-spirited Ajax, looking him in the eyes in the battle-cry of enemies, nor to fight him straight on, since he is stronger than you.”
sentences.n: ἀλλά … γε sets Hector against Ajax. ἐτάλασσας is a rare aorist (ἐτάλασσα) from the root of τλάω ‘endure, dare’, ‘you dared’, with the infinitives στήμεναι (= στῆναι) and μαχέσασθαι; Αἴαντος μεγαλήτορος ‘great-spirited Ajax’ is in the genitive because ἄντα ‘against’ governs it. κατ’ ὄσσε ἰδών ‘looking in the eyes’ is face to face; δηΐων ἐν ἀϋτῇ ‘in the battle-cry of enemies’. ἰθύς ‘straight on’. σέο is the epic genitive of σύ, the genitive of comparison after φέρτερος ‘stronger’. The speech ends at the edition’s full stop.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἄρ’ ὑπόδρα ἰδὼν προσέφη κορυθαίολος Ἕκτωρ·
sentences.l: Him then with a scowl looking addressed Hector of the glancing helmet:
sentences.i: Then Hector of the glancing helmet, looking at him with a scowl, spoke to him:
sentences.n: This is a formula for a reply with the speaker’s name changed; the line with Hector is also 12.230. ὑπόδρα ἰδών ‘looking with a scowl’ (the derivation of ὑπόδρα is not certain), προσέφη ‘addressed’ (an unaugmented aorist), and κορυθαίολος ‘of the glancing helmet’ is Hector’s stock epithet. Here it introduces Hector’s answer to Glaucus.

sentences.t: Γλαῦκε τί ἢ δὲ σὺ τοῖος ἐὼν ὑπέροπλον ἔειπες;
sentences.l: “Glaucus, why indeed, you, being such a one, arrogantly have you spoken?
sentences.i: “Glaucus, why have you, a man such as you are, spoken so arrogantly?
sentences.n: Hector’s answer starts with an indignant question to Glaucus. τί ἢ δέ is as the edition prints it; the particles are hard to pin down, but they sharpen the question. τοῖος ἐών ‘being such a one’ is the man Hector took him for, as the next line says. ὑπέροπλον is a neuter adjective used as an adverb, ‘arrogantly’, kin to ὑπεροπλίη ‘arrogance’; its formation is not clear. ἔειπες is the aorist of εἶπον with the epic ε-.

sentences.t:
ὢ πόποι ἦ τ’ ἐφάμην σὲ περὶ φρένας ἔμμεναι ἄλλων
τῶν ὅσσοι Λυκίην ἐριβώλακα ναιετάουσι·
sentences.l:
Ah! Truly I thought you in wits to be beyond others,
of those as many as Lycia, rich-soiled, inhabit;
sentences.i: Ah! Truly I thought you surpassed the others in wits, of all those who dwell in rich-soiled Lycia;
sentences.n: ὢ πόποι ‘ah!’ is an exclamation of dismay. ἦ τ’ ‘truly’, and ἐφάμην is the imperfect of φημί used for ‘thought’. σὲ περὶ φρένας ἔμμεναι ἄλλων: περί here is an adverb, ‘beyond’, with the genitive ἄλλων, and φρένας is an accusative of respect, ‘to be beyond others in wits’; ἔμμεναι is εἶναι. τῶν ὅσσοι … ναιετάουσι ‘of those, as many as dwell in’, ναιετάουσι being ναιετῶσι uncontracted. ἐριβώλακα ‘rich-soiled’ is from ἐρι- ‘very’ and βῶλος ‘clod’.

sentences.t:
νῦν δέ σευ ὠνοσάμην πάγχυ φρένας οἷον ἔειπες,
ὅς τέ με φῂς Αἴαντα πελώριον οὐχ ὑπομεῖναι.
sentences.l:
But now of you I find fault with altogether the wits, such a thing you have said,
you who say that I huge Ajax did not stand firm against.
sentences.i: But now I find fault with your wits altogether, what a thing you have said, you who say that I did not stand firm against huge Ajax.
sentences.n: Line 173 is the line at 14.95. ὠνοσάμην is the aorist of ὄνομαι ‘find fault with’, σευ the epic genitive of σύ, and φρένας ‘wits’ the part of Glaucus found fault with; πάγχυ ‘altogether’. οἷον ἔειπες ‘what a thing you have said’ is an exclamation. ὅς τέ με φῂς ‘you who say that I’ picks up σευ; φῂς is φῄς ‘you say’, with με … οὐχ ὑπομεῖναι, the aorist infinitive of ὑπομένω, ‘did not stand firm against’, and Αἴαντα πελώριον ‘huge Ajax’.

sentences.t: οὔ τοι ἐγὼν ἔρριγα μάχην οὐδὲ κτύπον ἵππων·
sentences.l: Not at all do I shudder at battle nor at the din of horses;
sentences.i: I do not shudder at the battle, nor at the din of horses;
sentences.n: οὔ τοι ‘indeed not’. ἔρριγα is a perfect of ῥιγέω with the sense of a present, ‘shudder at’, taking the accusatives μάχην ‘battle’ and κτύπον ‘din, crash’; ἐγών is the epic ἐγώ. Hector answers the charge of cowardice by saying what he does not fear.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ αἰεί τε Διὸς κρείσσων νόος αἰγιόχοιο,
ὅς τε καὶ ἄλκιμον ἄνδρα φοβεῖ καὶ ἀφείλετο νίκην
ῥηϊδίως, ὁτὲ δ’ αὐτὸς ἐποτρύνει μαχέσασθαι.
sentences.l:
but always the mind of Zeus is stronger, aegis-bearing,
who both the valiant man puts to flight and takes away victory
easily, and at another time himself urges him on to fight.
sentences.i: But the mind of aegis-bearing Zeus is always the stronger; he puts even the valiant man to flight and easily takes his victory away, and at another time himself urges a man on to fight.
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ αἰεί τε ‘but always’ states a general truth (the τε); Διὸς κρείσσων νόος ‘the mind of Zeus is stronger’, with αἰγιόχοιο ‘aegis-bearing’ as the stock epithet. ὅς τε ‘who’ is Zeus: φοβεῖ is present ‘puts to flight’ and ἀφείλετο a gnomic aorist, ‘takes away’, so both are what he always does; ῥηϊδίως ‘easily’. Line 177 is the line at 16.689. ὁτὲ δ’, with the accent as printed, is ‘at another time’ and answers an unspoken ‘at one time’; at 16.690 the nearly identical words are the conjunction ὅτε ‘when’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγε δεῦρο πέπον, παρ’ ἔμ’ ἵστασο καὶ ἴδε ἔργον,
ἠὲ πανημέριος κακὸς ἔσσομαι, ὡς ἀγορεύεις,
ἦ τινα καὶ Δαναῶν ἀλκῆς μάλα περ μεμαῶτα
σχήσω ἀμυνέμεναι περὶ Πατρόκλοιο θανόντος.
sentences.l:
But come, here, good one, stand beside me and see the deed,
whether all day long base I shall be, as you say,
or someone even of the Danaans, though greatly eager for might,
I shall check from warding off, about Patroclus dead.”
sentences.i: But come here, my good fellow, stand beside me and watch what I do, and see whether I shall be a coward all day long, as you say, or whether I shall stop some Danaan, however eager for might, from defending the body around dead Patroclus.”
sentences.n: Hector’s challenge. Line 179 is the Odyssey’s line at 22.233. παρ’ ἔμ’ ἵστασο ‘take your stand beside me’ and ἴδε ‘see’ are imperatives. ἠέ … ἦ opens a double question, ‘whether … or’. ἔσσομαι is the future of εἰμί, πανημέριος ‘all day long’, and κακός here is a bad fighter, a coward. ὡς ἀγορεύεις ‘as you say’ answers Glaucus. τινα … μεμαῶτα is a perfect participle, ‘eager’, with ἀλκῆς ‘for might’ in the genitive; μάλα περ ‘however greatly’. σχήσω is the future of ἔχω, ‘I shall check’, with the infinitive ἀμυνέμεναι ‘from warding off’; the object, the body, is left to be understood. περὶ Πατρόκλοιο θανόντος ‘around dead Patroclus’.

sentences.t: ὣς εἰπὼν Τρώεσσιν ἐκέκλετο μακρὸν ἀΰσας·
sentences.l: So having spoken, to the Trojans he called out, shouting loudly:
sentences.i: So he spoke, and gave orders to the Trojans, shouting loudly:
sentences.n: ὣς εἰπών ‘so having spoken’ closes Hector’s speech to Glaucus. ἐκέκλετο ‘called out, gave orders’ is the reduplicated aorist of κέλομαι. μακρὸν ἀΰσας ‘shouting loudly’: μακρόν is adverbial and ἀΰσας the aorist participle of ἀΰω ‘shout’.

sentences.t:
Τρῶες καὶ Λύκιοι καὶ Δάρδανοι ἀγχιμαχηταί,
ἀνέρες ἔστε φίλοι, μνήσασθε δὲ θούριδος ἀλκῆς,
ὄφρ’ ἂν ἐγὼν Ἀχιλῆος ἀμύμονος ἔντεα δύω
καλά, τὰ Πατρόκλοιο βίην ἐνάριξα κατακτάς.
sentences.l:
“Trojans and Lycians and Dardanians, close-fighters,
men be, friends, and be mindful of impetuous might,
until I the gear of blameless Achilles put on,
fine, which I despoiled, the might of Patroclus having killed.”
sentences.i: “Trojans and Lycians and Dardanians, you fighters at close quarters, be men, friends, and remember impetuous might, until I have put on the fine gear of blameless Achilles, which I stripped off when I killed the might of Patroclus.”
sentences.n: Hector calls on his own side. ἀγχιμαχηταί ‘close-fighters’ goes with all three names. ἀνέρες ἔστε φίλοι ‘be men, friends’ is a call to courage (the same words as 6.112); μνήσασθε is the aorist imperative of μιμνήσκομαι, with θούριδος ἀλκῆς ‘impetuous might’ in the genitive. ὄφρ’ ἂν … δύω: δύω is not ‘two’ here but the aorist subjunctive of δύω ‘put on’, and with ὄφρ’ ἂν the clause says ‘until I have put on’; ἔντεα … καλά ‘fine gear’ is its object. Ἀχιλῆος has the single λ for the metre, and the sense of ἀμύμων is not known. ἐνάριξα is ἐναρίζω ‘strip a slain man’. Πατρόκλοιο βίην ‘the might of Patroclus’ is a periphrasis for Patroclus himself, the object of κατακτάς, the aorist participle of κατακτείνω ‘kill’.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἄρα φωνήσας ἀπέβη κορυθαίολος Ἕκτωρ
δηΐου ἐκ πολέμοιο·
sentences.l:
So then, having spoken, went away Hector of the glancing helmet
out of the hostile war;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and Hector of the glancing helmet went off out of the hostile war;
sentences.n: Line 188 is also the line at 6.116, but there the sentence stops at Ἕκτωρ; here the edition prints no stop, and it runs on into 189. ἀπέβη ‘went away’; δηΐου ἐκ πολέμοιο ‘out of the hostile war’, where δήϊος ‘hostile’ is the same word as in 148.

sentences.t:
θέων δ’ ἐκίχανεν ἑταίρους
ὦκα μάλ’ οὔ πω τῆλε ποσὶ κραιπνοῖσι μετασπών,
οἳ προτὶ ἄστυ φέρον κλυτὰ τεύχεα Πηλεΐωνος.
sentences.l:
and running he overtook his companions
very quickly, not yet far, with rushing feet following after,
who to the town were carrying the famous armour of Peleus’-son.
sentences.i: He ran and quickly overtook his companions, who were not yet far off, following after them on rushing feet; they were carrying the famous armour of the son of Peleus to the town.
sentences.n: θέων ‘running’; ἐκίχανεν is the imperfect (here ‘overtook, came up with’) of κιχάνω ‘reach’, and ἑταίρους are the Trojans who have the armour. ὦκα μάλ’ ‘very quickly’ and οὔ πω τῆλε ‘not yet far off’ go with it. ποσὶ κραιπνοῖσι ‘with rushing feet’; μετασπών ‘following after’ is a compound of μετά with the stem of ἕπομαι ‘follow’. οἳ … φέρον ‘who were carrying’ with κλυτὰ τεύχεα Πηλεΐωνος ‘the famous armour of Peleus’-son’, the armour of Achilles that Hector gave them at 130–131.

sentences.t: στὰς δ’ ἀπάνευθε μάχης πολυδακρύου ἔντε’ ἄμειβεν·
sentences.l: and standing apart from battle of many tears his gear he was exchanging;
sentences.i: and, standing apart from the battle of many tears, he exchanged his gear;
sentences.n: στάς ‘having halted’; ἀπάνευθε ‘apart from’, with the genitive μάχης. πολυδάκρυος ‘of many tears’ is a compound of πολύ- ‘much’ and δάκρυ ‘tear’. ἔντε’ is ἔντεα ‘gear’, and ἄμειβεν is an unaugmented imperfect, ‘was exchanging’; what the exchange is, the next lines say.

sentences.t:
ἤτοι ὃ μὲν τὰ ἃ δῶκε φέρειν προτὶ Ἴλιον ἱρὴν
Τρωσὶ φιλοπτολέμοισιν,
sentences.l:
Indeed he, on the one hand, his own gear gave to carry to sacred Ilium
to the war-loving Trojans,
sentences.i: Hector, on the one hand, gave his own gear to the war-loving Trojans to carry to sacred Ilium,
sentences.n: ἤτοι ὃ μέν … ὃ δέ (the second half is at 194) sets the two halves of the exchange side by side, with Hector as the subject of both. τὰ ἃ is the demonstrative τά and the possessive ἅ ‘his own’, not a relative. δῶκε is an unaugmented aorist, φέρειν an infinitive of purpose, and προτὶ Ἴλιον ἱρήν ‘to sacred Ilium’. Τρωσὶ φιλοπτολέμοισιν ‘the war-loving Trojans’: φιλοπτόλεμος is φίλος with πτόλεμος, the epic form of πόλεμος.

sentences.t:
ὃ δ’ ἄμβροτα τεύχεα δῦνε
Πηλεΐδεω Ἀχιλῆος ἅ οἱ θεοὶ Οὐρανίωνες
πατρὶ φίλῳ ἔπορον·
sentences.i: and he, on the other hand, put on the deathless armour of Achilles, son of Peleus, which the gods of heaven gave to his dear father;
sentences.n: δῦνε is an unaugmented imperfect of δύνω ‘put on’. ἄμβροτα ‘deathless’ is said of the armour as the gift of gods, and Πηλεΐδεω Ἀχιλῆος is ‘Achilles, son of Peleus’ with the epic genitive -εω. ἅ is now the relative ‘which’ (the possessive of 193 is ἃ), and οἱ goes with πατρὶ φίλῳ, ‘to his dear father’, Peleus. Οὐρανίωνες ‘the Uranians’ are the gods of heaven, and ἔπορον is an aorist ‘gave’.

sentences.t:
ὃ δ’ ἄρα ᾧ παιδὶ ὄπασσε
γηράς·
sentences.l:
and he then to his own son bestowed,
having grown old;
sentences.i: and he, when he had grown old, passed them on to his own son;
sentences.n: ὃ δ’ ἄρα ‘and he in turn’ is Peleus. ᾧ is the possessive ‘his own’, not a relative, and ὄπασσε ‘bestowed’ is the aorist of ὀπάζω; the thing given, the armour, is left to be understood. γηράς is the aorist participle of γηράσκω, ‘having grown old’, in its epic form.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ οὐχ υἱὸς ἐν ἔντεσι πατρὸς ἐγήρα.
sentences.l: but the son in his father’s gear did not grow old.
sentences.i: but the son did not grow old in his father’s armour.
sentences.n: The poet’s own comment closes the part. ἐν ἔντεσι πατρός ‘in his father’s gear’ means wearing it, and ἐγήρα ‘grew old’ comes from the same root as γηράς in the line before. The armour passes from the gods to Peleus to Achilles, and the line says that Achilles did not grow old in it. Hector, meanwhile, now wears it.
